utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I call the case number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam [Realtime transcript read in error "Macedonia apple"] Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I like this if you see the transcript it says good morning, Macedonia apple Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can. Once again, good morning, Your Honours, yes, I can follow you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova and Denise Gustin, case manager. Mr. Nicholls will join us a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good morning to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Milan Trbojevic. I'm an attorney at law. Appearing today with my colleague Ms. Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you, too. So let's continue from where we left yesterday. Sir, I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And Madam Richterova will be continuing with her --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Trbojevic will go ahead with his cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you a couple of questions in order to clarify certain things. In your statement that you gave on the 14th of March, 2000, page 2, paragraph 3, you spoke about previous departures of the citizens, and you also described how the situation became increasingly exacerbated. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the date and the year of the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 14th of March, 2000. That's at least the date that I see on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, if you're going to ask questions on his statement, he should be provided with a copy of it, please, usher. Page and line, please? Page 2, paragraph 3, in the Serbo-Croat version or in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Witness, go to page 2, paragraph 3, please. And you are being reminded, supposedly, that you spoke about previous departures of the citizens, and how you particularly describe how the situation became increasingly exacerbated and you are being asked whether you remember that. Yes, now, your question, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this portion of your statement, it is indicated that Serb soldiers were going there and back, that they were the ones who had lots of weapons and did a lot of shooting around. Now I want to know whether there were any mobilised or non-mobilised soldiers who were members of the Muslim or Croat community, and who also appeared in the area with weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Muslim or Croat community, with weapons, either mobilised or not, were not in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that there were citizens of Muslim ethnicity who were members of Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P1679, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But this is one of the documents which belongs to the witness which was mentioned by Julian Nicholls on the previous occasions and we cannot use this documents in open session. These documents should be used only with the witness 7.144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And not with other witnesses. And in fact, it's not only that the document should be used in private or closed session, it shouldn't be distributed or shown other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me have a copy of the document itself. Is it on the ELMO already or not yet? Not yet, okay. Madam Registrar, could we have a copy of it because this has not been indicated before. Has this been used by any other witness already?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. And if you can go to the last page you can see the signature of the person I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Page 5. And it should be used only with the witness. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position is very simple. First of all this document has not yet been tendered in evidence as an exhibit. That's number 1. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. It's only preexhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So the fact that it has a number P1679 means nothing for the time being because it has not yet been tendered in evidence and that means that you cannot make use of it unless you try to tender it yourself, and you cannot tender it yourself because it is one of those protected privileged documents coming from an UN -- we'll redact that but it's a privilege from an UN agency so you need to take that into consideration, Mr. Trbojevic, you cannot make use of it. We can only make use of it actually if Mr. Whoever what is his name will be taking the witness stand next week or the week after will tender it in evidence and even then its use will be very limited and needs to be in closed session in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to quote several sentences as a foundation for my question for the witness. We don't have to know the author of this report. It doesn't have to be in closed session. I just asked whether there were any Muslims in Croatian army and here, it says that such and such a formation joined this other formation and covered a certain amount of the territory and so on and so forth. And I need just a few sentences from this report. I don't need to mention the author of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you cannot because this is a privileged document which, for all intents and purposes, has not yet even been tendered into evidence. Yes. So your answer is a very clear no. You can put any question you like but not with specific reference to this document or even expect to show the document to the witness. You can put the question in this form: We have information that. Do you confirm or do you not confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the President of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very pleased with what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report that will be part of the -- of the record when we hear this witness. It has nothing to do with you but it will be considered as an official document. The crux of the case being the fact that mention was made of Muslim units who joined Croatian units in the relevant area with the purpose of dividing this area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is just a lie and fabrication, because I was there in the area, I was present in all those locations, and you, you have just heard about it, you have just read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown one of our reports, P0671, a domestic report, if I can call it that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, next time please do give us an indication of what documents or exhibits you are going to make use of in the course of your cross-examination, because as it is, we come to this sitting completely without any of the documents that you intend using, especially if they are documents coming from other municipalities, you know, such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I am aware of the fact that this is my obligation. However, this belongs to the new binder that's been provided to us by the Prosecution and this is why I was convinced that you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 0671?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report to the main staff of the VRS by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps of the 9th of June, 1992. Under item 1, paragraph 2, we see the following: "From the territory of the Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Bosanski Novi municipalities, members of the green berets, who were broken into groups, that were fragmented into smaller groups are attempting to pull out and move into Cazin Krajina. There is a possibility that in the municipality of Kotor Varos, the Green Berets and HOS, Croatian Defence forces members, will commit provocations opening a new trouble spot."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in municipality of Bosanski Novi not in Kotor Varos, so I object this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you finished with your question, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one more sentence, Your Honour that I wish to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish with the question first and see whether it is relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, under paragraph 3, the last sentence, if you would be so kind and have a look at it, please? Just before item number 4, states as follows: "In the area of Mount Kozara and Mount Grmec there are about 300 members of green berets, who are attempting to get to Cazin Krajina in groups." That's what we read here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we can read here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: Does it follow from this report that in this border area, inside the town of Novi and around the town, Muslim or Croatian units could be found, as it is stated in this document? Were these units there at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm very sorry but I have to say that this sounds ridiculous to me. This report is dated the 9th of June, 1992. The entire population of that area had already been displaced and evicted by that day. Men were in camps, women were taken to Croatia or some other countries, so this mention of men who are fleeing towards Croatia could only refer to some individual cases of people who were afraid and wanted to escape from the area. The mention of green berets and some other armies or soldiers is pure fabrication and a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the local issues in Novi. You told us that the majority of Muslims had been dismissed from work. Do you remember stating that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the names of the people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is actually true that this was the consequence of a general situation? Most of the companies had to stop working because able-bodied Serbs had joined the military, the supplies were cut off, there was no electricity, and practically speaking, the industry, the economy, could not properly function? Would you agree with me that that was the general situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, then, that the companies continued to work normally but Muslim workers were dismissed from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that power shortages were very frequent at the time, that the electricity was cut off more often than not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether it was cut off more often than not, what the ratio was, I don't remember. I don't think it was 50/50 but I know that one part of the area was particularly affected by power shortages and -- but I don't know what the percentage would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation with fuel? Is it true that there was no fuel or that there was very little fuel at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, the situation was already very difficult and one could not normally obtain fuel, which means that you had to rely on the black market, and similar so-called businesses. The profiteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to come to the conclusion that some of the companies stopped working because of the power shortages, because of the fuel shortage, and because the supply lines towards Sarajevo, Belgrade and Zagreb were severed, and that that was in essence the reason why some of the companies stopped working.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that can only be your conclusion. As far as I'm concerned, the profiteers had as much fuel as they wanted to but they just wanted to keep the prices very high so that they could make money, because of the situation. Well, of course, if the situation was such, then the companies could not function normally, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that there were a lot of checkpoints in the area, but that these checkpoints were manned by local residents whom you more or less knew and you were able to go through these checkpoints without being controlled or searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that only unknown individuals were stopped at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't spend my time sitting on those checkpoints. I don't know what they did with other people. I told you about myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 9, you state that Mr. Hajro Nakic had left in a convoy and thus saved himself. Can you give us some more explanation, please? What convoy did he join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard. I heard that he went from the camp, Trnopolje, together with a convoy but as to how, I really don't know. And what I said about him saving his neck, I said because I knew that Serb soldiers were looking for him, probably because they wanted to do him as much harm as they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony yesterday at one point that somebody named Gojko Ostojic, I believe you said, went to talk to the soldiers, and when he came back, he informed you that it was dangerous for you to stay in a group in Donji Agici because that would make you dangerous even for the local population. Who did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said. At that moment, I was thinking that that's what it meant for those Serbs in Donji Agici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I conclude, then, that even those Serbs from Donji Agici were afraid of the shelling, that they too could be targeted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot make that conclusion. My conclusion was that he simply meant that they wanted us to go in order to avoid problems with the army for the Serbs and perhaps other citizens in Donji Agici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you described that on two occasions, you went to Donja Puharska, if I remember this correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Donja Puharska directly from Donji Agici, that is on the 12th of May, and after my release from the fire department camp, that is on the 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me about the road from Novi to Donja Puharska? Was it free of checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road from Novi to Prijedor was interspersed with checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you pass through them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With stopovers in Blagaj and the regular control, without stopping in Svodna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that it was possible to go through these checkpoints easily, without problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why you insist on making conclusions. I cannot make any conclusions. I'm only speaking on my behalf about events and cases I'm aware of personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll concentrate on you personally. Did you have any problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I was mistreated on checkpoints in Blagaj and in Svodna I already told you I didn't have to undergo a check at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Jusuf Ramic in Donja Puharska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (Redacted)no one (Redacted) Donja Puharska (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is that according to certain information, one of the headquarters of Territorial Defence was located in Donja Puharska and this Jusuf Ramic was its leader. Your trips to Donja Puharska are not related to that, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. You are again mentioning pure lies and fabrications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, please, I think we ought to redact his previous answer, the one which answered the question, do you know Jusuf someone in Donja Puharska? His answer, the witness's answer, ought to be redacted, okay? Yes, go ahead, Mr. Trbojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the time you spent at the stadium, did it ever happen that groups of soldiers coming back from the front line or combat actions attempted to enter the stadium and take their revenge on detainees or mistreat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at the stadium, and as far as I was able to see, that happened only once, when two soldiers, two armed soldiers, came and lined up all the detainees in single files, going from one to the other and telling us that they were looking for two Muslim men, and they named them. They didn't find these men and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, sorry, what has that got to do with football? How do you associate that with the question that was put to you, group of soldiers coming back from the front line or combat actions? Do you know that these two armed soldiers were coming from the front line? And why would they come to the football stadium if they were coming back from the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for whether they had come from the front line, I don't know that. All I know is that they were wearing military uniforms and carried automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it the first time that you saw soldiers wearing military uniforms and carrying automatic weapons in the stadium? Was it the only occasion? Or were there other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned this as a case that happened in the area of the stadium where we were located during daytime. It was on the turf of the stadium. Usually soldiers stayed outside, around the stadium and on the stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot testify about a single case when guards at the stadium prevented anyone from outside from entering the stadium and mistreating people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I didn't see anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the signing of those statements about leaving the municipality and transferring the title to one's property to the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that I did not mention this actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said that -- I remember him answering the question yesterday when he was asked whether he had signed anything, he said he never signed anything but that members -- other members of his family did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show the witness one of those statements and ask him to read it. Can I have document P1627, please? I'd like to have it shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to read this document? You don't have to read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to refuse to read this, if I may, because I'd never seen a statement of this sort. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is to look at it and tell me if signing away one's property is mentioned anywhere in this document, whether in the form of donation, transfer of ownership, relinquishing, whatever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, sir, this text is drafted by your side and was only signed by our people. What it means for me is that people had to sign this if they wanted to save their necks and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says no where in this document that they had to give up their property and give it away?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it makes no difference, the fact that he has not seen it before makes no difference. He is being asked to look at it today and state whether that document contains a declaration that property is being renounced to -- in favour of the Republika Srpska. And he's expected to say yes or no. Look at the document. If it says so, say yes, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it says so. If it doesn't say so, say no it doesn't say so. And if you have any remarks like you had just a couple of minutes ago, then you are perfectly entitled to make them too. But it's a perfectly legitimate question. It doesn't mean to say that if this document doesn't say that there is property being abandoned in favour of Republika Srpska, that in effect it wasn't. There may have been other documents and other decrees, orders, municipal decrees, laws or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What this document says is that one renounces for good one's property for the purpose of leaving the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hearby declare that I own no real estate in Bosanski Novi municipality under my own name and that I'm permanently leaving Bosanski Novi municipality." That means in my book that anyone who had any property or perhaps had some property did not dare to admit to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't be needing this document again, thank you. Can this witness be shown his own statement dated 12th of August, 1999? Could you please look at it? Do you see your own signature on each page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just mention by the way that in the heading, in the header of the statement, your name and country of residence are mentioned? So we should take care not to mention them. Could you tell me where was this statement done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says on the cover page, it was done in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the cover page, we see the title of the agency and its headquarters. Do you mean to say that you were in Sanski Most on the day when this statement was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Sanski Most on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at page -- there are no page numbers here but the ERN number is 00935059, in the top, right corner. That's page 3. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that number, but I can see page 3, the third page in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is another number here ending in 774. In the first third of the page, the sentence beginning with the words, "At the fire department in Bosanski Novi, more than 20 inmates were killed." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain this in greater detail? Because according to what you said, there were 15 of you plus 4 that you had found in the Una Hotel. That makes 19. So how did you come to this number of 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad you asked this question. Yesterday I had no time to mention this. From the beginning of the second week of our stay at the fire department camp, they brought every day or every other day, sometimes two, sometimes one, sometimes even three, new Muslim men in all sorts of vehicles, and in all sorts of ways. Every newcomer would be said to have been captured behind Matkovici and they said that this newcomer had been as far as Dvor and had been captured, and since there were no camps there, everybody was brought to the fire department camp. Also, there were a lot of civilians captured between Prijedor and Bosanski Novi. Also, while attempting to cross over the border to Croatia. All these civilians were kept between one and three days on that location. Within that time, they would beat them up badly so as to almost disable them before they drove them away, and these people never returned. So this figure here is not only correct but it could be even higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, these are people who were brought to the Vatrogasni Dom and taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you how they were brought in. Sometimes in the trunk of the car. Once they brought three men in the trunk of a small Volkswagen Golf. All three were blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me a bit further down below, in that statement, it says that the vice-president of the SDA party, it says the following night Resad Berberovic, the secretary of the SDA and Abdulah Huzeirovic from Blagaj were taken away and beaten. Zeljko Bosancic, Janjetovic and Djuric, who drove the military police van took them away. Now comes your explanation. Resad and Abdulah were killed on that occasion. Zoran Maric from Maricka in Prijedor municipality killed Abdulah on the bridge over the Sana River in Blagaj. He was shot and found in a bush by women, whereas Resad Berberovic was killed somewhere above the River Sana." Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I swear to this because I know this personally, that they were taken away and killed, and as for the fact that they were killed somewhere above the River Sana is something I heard and I could suppose that much after Isakovic's murder. Plus the fact that they have not been found to this day. That tells me that they probably have never been buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you eye witnessed when they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken away before my very eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you take this description from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it something that you heard from someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from the families of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does Maric, Zoran fit in here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military policeman from Prijedor who was in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he at the fire department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a military policeman at the fire department. If I say military policeman, that's -- I mean one of the people who were at the fire department. I knew Abdulah Huzeirovic because we met two or three years previously at the football field. He was the goalkeeper. In fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Maric was acquainted with Huzeirovic, they knew each other as football players. One was centre field and the other was goalkeeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned that were you beaten, you mentioned baseball bats as one of the instruments.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you really mean it or did you simply mean some wooden sticks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly meant it, I'm sorry to say, and as far as I know, baseball bats are made of wood, and I saw such bats being broken on the backs of inmates. Two Salkic brothers were especially badly beaten with these bats. They were brothers from Urije and it all happened in this period that I talked about 15 minutes ago. The Salkic brothers belonged to the group of people who have never been heard from since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because baseball bats were not on sale in shops. It's not something that you could buy, and we were not familiar with baseball bats except from movies. How come they were so common in Bosanski Novi at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you really want to know, why don't you ask your soldiers? They brought them from somewhere apparently. That's all I can say in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any explanation for the fact that from Mlakve stadium, just from hundreds of men, just a group of 15 was taken to the fire station and kept there for such a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they said they had received those lists from higher authorities and that we would be questioned at the hotel. Later on, they were kept -- we were kept at the hotel for only three days before being transferred to the fire department, and there we gave statements similar to those that we had previously given at Keraterm and in Bosanski Novi. So no particular charges were brought against me personally, and I don't think anyone else was ever charged, including those people who are missing to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: As you lived together and became to know each other, could you trace any common denominator, for example that there were allegedly rich people or educated people or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was released, of course I thought about it all, and it was perhaps possible to reach a conclusion of some sort, because, for instance, me and my two friends from Gornji Agici, just as two acquaintances from Suhaca and Slovare, we all had parents working in Germany. The vice-president and the secretary of the SDA, whom I mentioned before, as well as Ismet Muslimovic, were, according to their stories, detained because of the positions -- they were left behind because of the positions that they had. I don't know what happened with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the following names? And if you have, did you know these persons? Camil Alic? Fehim, Mehmedagic, Samir Izmirevic? Did you know of any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Camil Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see him at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other two persons you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you at any time during your stay in the stadium come across a certain person by the name of Balaban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone nicknamed Trnka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may make a correction, he was nicknamed Trnika [phoen]. I knew him because I was able to see him from time to time on the buses of the Kozaraprevoz company from Bosanski Novi. He worked there as a conductor for a while and he also washed buses and did similar jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you didn't see him at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That brings us to the end of your testimony, which means that you can now return to your country of residence, to your home. For this purpose, you will be assisted, given all the assistance you require by the officers of this Tribunal, but before you leave this courtroom it is my duty as the Presiding Judge in my name and on behalf of the two Judges that sit with me in this trial, and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, to thank you for having accepted to come over to give evidence in this trial. Thank you and you will now be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have 7.66 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 7.66 enjoys the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Pseudonym and image distortion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly so we can stay as we are but in open session. Do you expect this witness to take the rest of the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's likely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make sure that we finish with all these witnesses by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I make sure that Your Honours have everything? We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have what weave given which is basically the statement (Redacted) -- sorry, it is 2nd February, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then 26 June, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus a diagram, plus another statement of the 8 April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus a list of what could be documents, exhibits, that could be made use of and these are the attachments that come with the two statements and the P1683 Bosanski Novi photos. And please, Madam Registrar, redact from the records the initial part of my intervention, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think you've been given a supplemental information sheet for Witness 7.66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm going to refer, but before I do that, I'm referring to line 22 -- page 22, line 8, where I put -- where I mention a date. But before I mention the date of the statement, I mentioned another date and that ought to be redacted, just out of precaution. Then you are right, we have a supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, that's an error. There shouldn't be one for this witness. That's for my next witness, if everybody can disregard that? It's got the wrong witness number on it. It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what number would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll redistribute it with the correct number and that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm tearing it, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That will be -- 7.88's will be virtually identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've never given evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore I'm going to explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. First thing that is going to happen is that you are going to make, to enter a solemn declaration, equivalent to the oath, to an oath, that in the course of your testimony, you will be saying the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. This is required under our rules, before any witness starts giving evidence. The text of this solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that the usher, the gentleman who is standing to your left, will be handing to you. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be telling us the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. You know Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls is appearing for the Prosecution, as far as you are concerned, and he will be conducting what we refer to as the examination-in-chief. He will be asking you a series of questions to which you are requested to give an answer, a short, concise but precise answer. Don't answer more than you are asked. The formula is a very simple one. You just answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. If you don't, you are only make matters worse. We will have problems. You will be here for days on end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After that, you will be asked questions on cross-examination by the Defence counsel appearing for Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the defendant, who is the accused in this case. You have no right to make any distinction between Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Trbojevic. Both of them are here dining their duty and your responsibility is to answer all the questions put to you irrespective of who is putting the question in complete and truthful manner. So Mr. Nicholls will start with his examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first piece of business, I think, is to show the witness the first exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just look at that piece of paper, please, see whether your name is printed out correctly. Don't read it. Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So show that to the Defence counsel and to us. And that will become Exhibit P16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 31, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 31, and it will be received and kept under seal. Which leads me to the next point, sir, and that is when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, you asked for certain protective measures aimed mainly to protect your identity while you give evidence here. I think you already know that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- this Trial Chamber has accepted your request and you are being given protective measures as follows: First, you will not be referred to by your name but by a nom de plume, by a pseudonym. You are BT84? BT84. That's how you are known here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And not by your name. Secondly, you see that the back of you, there is a curtain plus a board. That is used to hide your identity. If you switch on video mode on your monitor, on video mode, you will see how you appear to the public who may be following these proceedings. They won't be able to see your face but they will be able to see that camouflage that you can notice now on your monitor. So that's what you asked for. That's what has been accepted by this Trial Chamber. Now, Mr. Nicholls will proceed with the questions. And for the first part of the questions, we go into private session, which means that the public won't even be hearing your voice and what you will be saying for the first series of questions, which will deal with who you are and where you come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the map that we have been using, P1624.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at that map for a moment, I showed that to you earlier. Could you tell us whether that's a fair and accurate map of Bosanski Novi, of the municipality? You can look at it on -- where -- to your right, if that's easier than looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I think it's accurate enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point out Alici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: [indicates] Going from Bosanski Novi towards Blagaj Japra and Blagaj Rijeka, then you pass through the local community of Maslovare, which also includes Ekici and Alici and this is where Alici is located, between Suhaca and Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the ethnic composition of Alici at the end of 1991? Who lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Only Muslims lived in Alici and Ekici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the area you've pointed out on the map, you correct me if I'm wrong, but when you -- in the late 1980s, and up into 1991, relations between all of the people in that area was pretty good, relations between Serbs and non-Serbs, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: One couldn't complain. The relations were very good up until the beginning of the war in Croatia. At that time, one could already notice certain tensions. People no longer recognised each other on the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell me now about any radio broadcasts you heard, either at the end of 1991 or later on, which may or may not have increased these tensions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I listened to the music on the Bosanski Novi radio station on several occasions but I also listened to the news, and the music was usually accompanied by statements in which Muslims were referred to as terrorists, and there was already talk about the fact that Muslims had to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you first started hearing radio broadcasts stating that Muslims should surrender weapons? If you can put a month on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I don't think I can remember the month but it was at the very beginning, when Suhaca, Hozici and Agici, when the populations of these villages was displaced. So it was during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did these radio broadcasts state that Muslims should surrender their weapons or that all people should or civilians? Can you be a little bit more specific as to who was ordered to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. Reference was only to Muslims and Muslims extremists. That's what I personally heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember hearing on the radio that Muslims living in the villages around Alici should surrender weapons? And if you do, can you tell me which villages those were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. It was the entire valley of the Japra River, not only specific villages, Ekici or Alici but the entire area of the Japra River valley, that is the Muslim population of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally surrender any weapons on the basis of these radio broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I had a pistol for which I possessed a legally valid permit, but there appeared at one point in time some military police, and I gave this pistol to one of them. I don't know exactly who the person was but I know that the patrol was led by Rajko Karlica. I gave them the pistol and I wanted to keep the permit but he said that the pistol would be returned to me once the state becomes legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, let's tackle the bull by the horn straight away, because he's just mentioned a name Rajko Karlica, and in his second statement, namely the one of 26th of June, 2002, he says -- he corrects himself and says that it was wrong in mentioning this name, it should be another name. Could you just ask him whether he confirms the name Rajko Karlica or whether he wants to change it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, sir. Are you sure about that name, Rajko Karlica or is it possibly a different name, the name of the person you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. We didn't understand each other. I gave my pistol to a man whose name I don't know, but with this military police was also this person by the name of Zoran Karlica. As for Ranko Karlica, we will talk about him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you do. Be careful I won't allow you to put a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't ask the name. It's in the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to break fairly soon, sir, but could you tell me, slow down a little bit, and tell me how you came to be in this field, or the place where you surrendered the pistol and who else was there. Tell me how that came about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I was in the village of Ekici visiting Ferid Ekic in his house when this military police came in a patrol vehicle, in a jeep. They confiscated Ferid -- they hid his pistol. They confiscated all legally possessed pistols and as for this person, I gave him my pistol but before that, I had gone to my house on an APC to get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to seeing many people from different villages gathered as part of a process of surrendering weapons. Can you explain how you saw that? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: When the weapons were being handed over in Ekici, actually this happened only later. I saw here on the photograph the location. It was below one of -- below this house that people from Suhaca and Hozici, I don't know how many of them there were, but the group included women, children and men who had come on tractors and other vehicles to this location here, just below the house that you can clearly see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we should break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Let's have a 25-minute break. Thank you. Be careful that while the witness is going out, the rules are observed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be shown a photograph, P1683.16?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to continue to ask you some questions about the surrender of weapons from the villages of Alici and surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Usher, I don't know if you can -- if you could pull the whole, the ELMO back a little bit because I can't see the witness? Thanks, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a look at that photograph and tell me if you recognise it -- where that -- what is depicted there, where is that field and what is that house, that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I know this house very well. It still stands in the same place today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, if you want to point, you need to point not at your monitor but at the photo to your right. Sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I was saying, below that house, you can see the meadow where the people were gathered on that day. Over there, stands a monument from the First World War. This is a very familiar house. Somewhere here on the road, I saw Ranko Karlica, who was mentioned a little while ago. I don't believe that he was a leader of any kind. He was a simple soldier carrying a regular rifle. He was only obeying orders. It was on this road that I saw a tractor with a number of rifles on it, mostly hunting rifles, perhaps there was an army rifle among them. These weapons were about to be surrendered. The troops were going to Suhaca or Hozici. I couldn't see very well. Supposedly to search houses, look for weapons. I don't remember what exactly was their explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness his statement from April 2000 to the Office of the Prosecutor I'm showing the witness, it's been opened to page 3 which is the same section in both B/C/S and the English translation. Excuse me, the B/C/S translation and the English original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that the statement you gave earlier, sir? That's just a yes or no question. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes. This is my statement but I'm not sure whether this reference to Ranko is correct. I'm not sure Ranko was his name. Perhaps it was Rajko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you step by step. You're jumping ahead a little bit but that's what I was going to ask you about. In the third paragraph down which begins, "When I came to Maslovare, I saw 10 to 15 Serb soldiers dressed up in olive uniforms, olive green uniforms." Couple of sentences later it states, "He was Rajko Karlica and was a driver by profession and drove a bus in Dvor Croatia." Now, I think what you just told me is you're not sure that the first name is correct. Did I understand you correctly, that you're not sure about the first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes. I think his name is Ranko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the last name? Are you sure the last name is Karlica or do you think it might be something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes, his last name is Karlica. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that statement down now. That's okay. Now, when you were showing us the photo of the field and you were looking at it you said that the people were gathered there and you pointed to the meadow. Can you tell me which people these were? In other words, who were these people, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Those were people from Suhaca and Hozici, men, women, children, all the Muslims, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you present in that field with these other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I was there for about an hour and a half, maybe two hours, because I didn't belong with that group, because residents of Alici were not there in that field, only residents of Suhaca and Hozici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it only residents of Suhaca and Hozici? How did you know that? Who told you this is supposed to be residents of Suhaca and Hozici today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I don't know who said that, who gave that order. I was there by chance because I had been on my way to do some shopping and I found these people standing in the field. I stopped to talk to this Ranko Karlica and ask him what is going on? And he told me these people were from Suhaca and Hozici and they had come to surrender their weapons before they can go back home. I'm saying that I was free to move about. I wasn't ordered to be there that day. We in Ekici were sort of protected by these neighbours because they told us themselves that we are not guilty of anything, that we should leave Alici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me make sure that was correct. Your neighbours stated that you, the people of Alici, were not guilty of anything, and that you should leave Alici or should not leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. They told us that we should not go anywhere, that no harm would come to us, that nobody would touch us. However, things turned out differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get to that later. Can you just tell me which neighbours were these who told you that you would be safe there in Alici and you shouldn't leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I don't know if I dare mention the name but the sons --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to mention the names. Were these Serb neighbours from Serb-neighbouring villages? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. Those were our Serb neighbours and they told us there was no need for us to go anywhere like the residents of Suhaca and Hozici, that our hamlet would be left alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just before we move on, you talked about the citizens of Hozici and Suhaca who were in this meadow which you pointed out to us surrendering weapons. Were these all men, were they men, women and children? Can you describe the people briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who you saw in the field surrendering weapons, were those all men or were there also women and children there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: A couple of men were only involved in the surrender of weapons. Women had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the people who were in that field -- you said that you were free to move, that you were not held there. Were the other civilians you were -- who were held there, the people from these other villages, Suhaca and Hozici, were they free to leave, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. They were not free to leave. At least not for three or four hours. Those people stayed there for another three or four hours after I left. I heard that they returned to their homes only later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what was going on at their homes while they were being held in the meadow, in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: It's a funny question, it seems to me, because of course I can't know what was going on at their houses while they were there. I heard that their houses were searched, turned upside down, I don't know what they were looking for really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's fine. Now, after this search which you viewed, you said you were able to -- you were able to move around and you were able to leave. After this incident, were you -- did you -- were you -- could you continue to move freely as you wished throughout the area or did anything change to stop you from moving around Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: After this gathering, in the meadow, I personally was free to go about, to go to Bosanski Novi or anywhere else, but when Suhaca Hozici, Blagaj Japra and all the other villages were evacuated, when the residents went to Blagaj, in that period, I wasn't free to go to Suhaca, Hozici, Blagaj or anywhere else. During all that time, I stayed in Alici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when the people of Suhaca and Hozici were taken to Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I believe it's somewhere in the calendar for 1992. It must be marked somewhere. It may have been the 23rd or the 24th, May or June. I think it was May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could put the statement down, you don't need to look it up, that's all right. We can continue and I'll -- we'll get to the calendar later. In any event, when you saw -- can you tell me what you saw on that day when what happened to the people from Suhaca and Hozici and Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: That day, I happened to be visiting my father-in-law, and I saw people on tractors, vehicles, horse-drawn carts, from Suhaca, Hozici and other places driving to Bosanski Novi in a sort of convoy. It was a terrible sight to see people who were forced to release their animals from stables and abandon them. The animals were running wild, screaming. I simply can't make sense of it. It was a terrible scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you just give the Chamber an idea of the scale of the convoy that you saw? I don't -- I know you can't tell us exactly how many people were in it but how large was this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: The convoy, as far as I could see, because I really couldn't linger there, it was the first time I ever drove a tractor. It was the tractor belonging to my father-in-law. We loaded up our belongings and went to our house in Alici, but as far as I could see from a distance, it was a kilometre long, more or less. I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. And also on this day, the day of -- when all these people left their villages, did you see any damage to any of these villages, to any buildings in any of the villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: That day, when people were leaving their homes, I didn't see anything. I didn't see whether anyone was killed, whether anything was destroyed. That day I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the days after -- immediately after you saw this convoy leaving, did you see any damage to any of those villages, to any of the homes in those villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I wasn't allowed to go to Suhaca or Hozici. I knew there was no one in those villages, only robbers, looters went there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this convoy left, can you tell us briefly what life was like for people still living in Alici and Ekici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I can try. During that month, from the 23rd or 24th April, before this incident with Alici happened, everything was more or less all right. People came and told us that we should feel safe. They asked us if anyone was bothering us. Later on, things changed, but in the village of Josava, which you can see on the picture, somebody was allegedly killed, an officer or a commander, I don't know, but I believe that as far as this incident in Ekici is concerned, I think that someone named Bogdan Grab is responsible. I don't know this Bogdan Grab person because I moved into these parts from elsewhere. I wasn't a local.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you just, to clear up some dates, your statement from 2nd of February of this year. Just -- the one you've just made. I'm going to show you the last page, last attachment to that statement, which is a photocopy of a wallet calendar from 1992. It's marked KW/MB 14. And just look at that a second. Do you recognise that photocopy of the wallet calendar front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the side, which has markings on it, I'm sorry that the photocopy is not better quality but if you can look at that, do you recognise markings on the calendar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I do. So between the 23rd and the 24th was this convoy from Suhaca and Hozici to Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you a second and just explain what these markings are and you tell me if I'm correct. Under May, you've written "Suhaca" and marked the dates 23 and 24; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally write "Suhaca" there and mark those two dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes. This is my own signature, and I can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June, you've written "Alici" and marked the dates 22 and 23, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in July, you wrote "Karlovac" I believe and marked the dates 23 and 24?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Trial Chamber when you made these marks, when you marked these dates, and when you wrote the names of these places on your wallet calendar from 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I didn't dare make these markings in Bosanski Novi or Alici. Any document found on you was a danger. But when I went to Karlovac, around the 23rd or the 24th, I found this calendar somewhere and made these markings for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's fairly obvious but why did you make these markings? Why did you want to preserve these particular dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Simply because, how shall I put it? Because it's history, because I wanted to remember what happened, when I had to leave, when I went to Germany and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you kept this card with you since that time, in fact you still have this card, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I still have it. Unfortunately I didn't bring it here but I have it and I believe it is valuable proof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the markings for the 23rd and 24th of May where you wrote Suhaca, there, you were indicating the time that all the people left Suhaca and when you saw that convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that down now, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we should, if we may, go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember my question, can you tell me what you did next? Tell me what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If that could be, the diagram, P1632 under seal, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could continue and tell us what you did next? You had just started telling us about how the home was in flames, the animals had been set free. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: At that moment, I was still on the tree. There was -- there were -- the forest was green and I had a green track suit on so I was almost invisible. I did not climb down from the tree until 11.30 p.m. because the Serbian cemetery was located in the vicinity, not far from the place where I was. There were women and children there, and the distance between the tree and the cemetery was perhaps 150 metres as the crow flies so it was only at about 11.30 that I climbed down from the tree. After they had already left the cemetery. You could still hear the shooting but from afar. As I climbed down, after I climbed down from the tree, I went to the Serb cemetery. It was some 50 metres away from me, and I lay down in the grass there. There was no one in the vicinity. And I could see -- I could hear the shooting coming from the place where the massacre had taken place. It must have been around half past midnight or 1.00, I'm not sure. And it was only at about 3.30 or 4.00 in the morning when it dawned, and when I was able to see, that I started hearing the noise that tractors made. So I think that looting was going on at that time, although one could still hear individual shots, but I didn't notice anything. I then went in the direction of Meho Alic's house and further into the forest. Below this forest, I don't know how to explain this, I was just above the place where the massacre had taken place, some 500 metres away from the spot, and I could see some -- something which looked like sacks. I couldn't recognise anyone, but I'm sure that those were the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back a bit. In your statement, you heard at one point you heard women and children crying or screaming. And then later on, you heard villagers singing. Could you describe the singing and when that happened in the sequence of events and who was singing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: After the shooting, after I had already took shelter in the forest, that is right after I had locked up the house and when the shooting started, I fled into the forest and at that time I could hear screams and cries coming from this group of women and children while the shooting was going on at Johici [phoen] but I heard the singing for the first time when they were at the Serb cemetery. I couldn't hear everything clearly but I remember one particular song which went like this: "A Serb mother gave birth to," me and something along those lines, which was sung by those women and children who were gathered there and who were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point, did you see the men and the women and children of the villages separated? In other words, were the women and children brought one place or the men one other place at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I have to tell you first of all that I was not able to see them. I could only hear them. I could hear the noise of the tractors when women and children were boarding them, the tractors that eventually took them to the Urije neighbourhood in Bosanski Novi. As for the men, they were taken in the direction of Ranko Karlica's house down the road that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm sorry I would like to go back into private session and use this diagram again just to make it clear where the witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Private session, and usher, you can hand the previous diagram sketch to the witness, please, that's P1632.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll wait for the blinds to go up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me what happened after the shooting stopped. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: So this happened about 1.00, 1.30 after midnight. I remained hiding in the grass. You could hear sporadic shooting all around. I remained hiding in the grass until half past 3.00. It was early morning hours. It was cold and wet, and I was wearing only a track suit. I went back home, although nothing remained of my home, but there was a stable standing still, at least partially. I found a jacket in that stable. I put it on and went to Meho Alic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see on the way to Meho Alic's house? Did you see anything that you remember sticking out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: When I set out towards Meho Alic's house, I was actually going in the direction of Bosanski Novi through the woods, and passing by Meho Alic's stable, I saw a body lying in the ditch, wearing no shoes, only socks, lying face down. I turned the body over. I thought -- I saw it was Jusuf Alic. I saw it wasn't Jusuf Alic, Meho's brother. I saw it was Fadil Ekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, don't say their names but at this point, did you know where your family was? And what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: No. At that point, I didn't. It was only in the afternoon that I found out what happened with them. That is when I came to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do next after seeing Fadil Ekic's body in this ditch, in the canal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. I continued on my way towards this woods, in the direction of Bosanski Novi, and it was from the woods that I was able to see this massacre that happened near the Muslim cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say from the woods you could see this massacre that had happened, just please to be clear for the record, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: Well, I saw these bodies lying like sacks. I can't describe to you what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please continue and tell us, tell the Chamber how you made your way towards Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT84
utterances.text: So I made my way to Bosanski Novi through the woods. I ran into a patrol, or rather a checkpoint manned by the police or the army, I'm not sure. I didn't wait to run into them. I went around them towards a hamlet near Urije, and I went to visit Mustafa Alic. There I saw women and children in a group, and I asked them about my own wife and children, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but they were not to be found there. I called in another house of another man I knew, Hasib Alic. His daughter-in-law offered me coffee and a couple of cigarettes, and I felt relief for a moment. I asked again about my wife and children, but they couldn't tell me anything about them. I was lost. I didn't know where to go. I ran into another person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was told that translation in -- on page 54, line 6, does not correspond to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you bring that up when he's finished answering the question, not in the course of his answering the question. Let him finish first. That's not fair. It shouldn't be done that way. Yes, continue, sir. You were saying, "I called in another house of another man I knew, Hasib Alic, his daughter-in-law offered me coffee and a couple of cigarettes and I felt relief for a moment. I asked again about my wife and children but they couldn't tell me anything about them. I was lost. I didn't know where to go. I ran into another person." That's when you were stopped and you can continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't Hasan, it was Hasib Alic. Any way, as I was saying, I didn't know rightly where to go. At that moment another man came by and asked me who I was looking for. I said I was looking for my wife and children. He asked me, (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Redacted) And I went to the house to which he had directed me and found my wife and children there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we ought to redact where he says where he -- where he came from, all right? So that I don't repeat the name myself. We are talking of line 11 on this page, page 55. And line 12. Are you from that place? And he said, "Yes, I am." Go ahead. Before you go ahead, yes, what was your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was told that interpretation was not correct in line 6, page 54. It doesn't correspond to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
